lesson.menu_title: Going North — How a Company Is Taken Into a New Market
lesson.menu_desc: Reading: what actually happens when a Brazilian company opens in the United States -- 31 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- Going North
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 2 -- Going North

paras: Every year a few hundred Brazilian companies decide that the United States is the next market, and almost all of them are surprised by the same thing. It is not the competition, and it is not the language. It is that the country is not one market at all. A subsidiary is incorporated in one state, taxed under the rules of another, and sued under the law of a third, and none of that is unusual enough to be explained to you in advance.

The first decision is where the company is created. Delaware is chosen by most foreign groups, not because it is cheap, but because its company law is old, detailed and predictable, and because judges there have seen the argument before. The filings are made online in a morning. The bank account, which everybody assumes is the easy part, is where months are lost: the account is subject to checks that were designed for a different problem, and a company with no American track record is exactly what those checks were written to slow down.

Then comes the part nobody budgets for. Payroll is run under state rules that change at the border. Contracts that were drafted in Portuguese and translated are read by a counterparty who has never seen that structure. Work that used to be done in-house is outsourced simply because nobody in the head office has the certification the client asks for. None of this is red tape in the sense of somebody being obstructive. It is a different rulebook, applied by people who have no idea that yours exists.

The companies that get a foothold have one habit in common: they go small first, on purpose. One state, one product, one client who is willing to be the reference. The operation is only scaled once something has been sold twice to somebody who was not a friend of the founder. It is unglamorous, it is slow, and it is the only version of this story that is told by companies that are still there five years later.

listenings.text: People ask me how long it takes to set up in the United States, and I always give the same unhelpful answer: the company takes a morning and the rest takes a year. Incorporating is genuinely quick. The filings are made online, the certificate arrives, and everybody feels wonderful for about a week. Then you need a bank account, and the account is subject to checks that were written for money laundering, not for a media company from Sao Paulo with no American history. Nothing you say makes that faster. What makes it faster is having an American director, a real address that is not a mailbox, and a track record you can show on paper. My advice is boring and it is the only advice that works: start the banking on day one, in parallel with everything else, and assume it will be the thing that decides your launch date.

If I did it again, I would do one thing differently, and it is not the lawyers or the structure. I would refuse to launch in more than one state. We rolled out in four at once because it felt like ambition, and what we actually bought was four sets of payroll rules, four filing calendars and four different answers to the same question. We were not scaling. We were repeating the same small problem in four places and calling it growth. The foothold we eventually got came from a single client in a single state who agreed to be a reference, and everything after that was easier, because for the first time we had something to point at. Go small on purpose. It looks like caution from the outside, and from the inside it is the fastest route there is.

extra_audio.text: The company decides that the United States is the next market. A subsidiary is incorporated in Delaware, because the company law there is predictable. The filings are made online in a morning, and then the bank account takes months. Payroll, contracts and certification turn out to follow a different rulebook in every state. The operation is only scaled after the same thing has been sold twice to somebody outside the founder's circle.
